opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a topic I think about a lot, partly because I work on open models and a lot of the strongest open-weight models right now are coming out of Chinese labs. So I feel this tension pretty directly.

I take Dario seriously. He's thoughtful, and Anthropic has been consistent that they see AI as a national security issue and not only a product race. The core argument goes like this: if AI turns out to be as transformative as they believe, then who gets there first, and under what values, matters a lot. So they want democracies to keep a lead, and they back things like export controls on advanced chips. I don't think that position is crazy, and the compute argument especially has real substance. Access to frontier compute is one of the few levers anyone actually has.

Where I push back is on framing and on what the policy actually does. A few things:

First, the Chinese labs are very good. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, and others are doing excellent research, often with less compute, and they're publishing and releasing weights. If the message is "they're just copying" or "we can wall them off," I think that underestimates them and can lead to bad decisions. Talent there is real, and efficiency innovations happen partly because of the constraints.

Second, there's a risk that the safety and security argument gets used, intentionally or not, in ways that hurt open models generally, including American ones. If the policy conversation slides from "control the most advanced chips" to "open weights are dangerous because China benefits," then the U.S. ecosystem loses something important. Right now, a lot of researchers, startups, and universities around the world build on Chinese open models because they're the best available. I'd much rather the U.S. answer that by releasing great open models of its own than by trying to restrict the category.

Third, there's the incentive question, which people always raise with Anthropic. They're a frontier closed lab, so arguments that favor tighter controls also happen to line up with their commercial position. I don't think that means they're being cynical, and I think Dario genuinely believes what he says. But listeners should keep it in mind and look at the arguments themselves.

So my overall view is: the concern about the geopolitics of AI is legitimate, and compute policy is a reasonable thing to debate. But the most productive response isn't fear, it's competing. Invest in open research, fund academic compute, build American open models people actually want to use, and stay honest about how capable the Chinese ecosystem is. That's a stronger position than hoping restrictions alone keep us ahead.

r001.rationale: The response questions extending security arguments to open weights generally, but it does not judge Amodei’s warnings about near-term open-weight risks to be overly forceful.

r002.rationale: It discusses Chinese labs and talent, but does not mention Anthropic media statements distinguishing the Chinese government from individual Chinese scientists.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a few layers to this. Dario has been very consistent about this for years now, and I actually respect that he's willing to put his name on a position that's pretty unpopular in a lot of the research community. The core of his argument is that whoever gets to really powerful AI first gets to shape the world it's deployed into, and he'd rather that be democracies than the Chinese Communist Party. On the pure values question, I don't really disagree with him.

Where I get more uncomfortable is how that argument gets used. Export controls are the obvious example. Dario wrote a long piece after DeepSeek arguing the controls are working and need to be tightened, and I think the evidence is a lot more mixed than that. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, all these labs kept shipping very competitive models while being chip-constrained. If anything, the constraints made them more efficient and more motivated to open source, which has now put a lot of the best open weights in the world in Chinese hands. That's an outcome the policy was supposed to prevent, not accelerate.

The other thing I'd push on is the framing of this as a race with a finish line. A lot of the "China is six months behind" or "China is a year behind" discourse assumes there's a decisive moment where the gap matters enormously. I'm much more in the camp that this is a long, incremental diffusion of technology, and in that world the question isn't who's ahead by a quarter, it's who builds the ecosystem people actually want to use. Right now Chinese open models are winning a lot of developer mindshare globally because American labs mostly stopped releasing weights. That's a soft-power problem that the national-security framing tends to completely miss.

So my short version is: the concern about authoritarian control of transformative technology is legitimate, and I don't want to be dismissive of it. But I think some of the loudest warnings come bundled with policy prescriptions that benefit the people making them, and the US response of restricting and closing up rather than competing in the open has, so far, not obviously worked. I'd like to see us compete on being the better option, not just on denying the other side chips.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions export controls and race framing, but does not judge warnings about near-term risks from open-weight AI models to be overly forceful.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts democracies with the Chinese Communist Party but does not distinguish concerns about the Chinese government from views of individual Chinese scientists.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two things: whether there are legitimate security concerns around AI, and whether Dario’s framing of China is the right way to understand those concerns. You can take the first seriously without accepting the second wholesale.

He’s also the CEO of a company competing in this market, so I’d scrutinize those warnings rather than treat them as a neutral assessment. That doesn’t mean they’re insincere. It means we should ask what specific capability or behavior he’s worried about, what evidence supports that concern, and whether his proposed response would actually reduce the risk.

My concern with a broad US-versus-China framing is that it can make every advance look like a threat and every safety measure look like a competitive disadvantage. We should be able to discuss concrete security risks without making cooperation on safety impossible.

r001.rationale: The response questions Dario’s broad China framing but does not discuss open-weight models, near-term risks, or judge his warnings about them as overly forceful.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Anthropic media statements or distinguish the Chinese government from individual Chinese scientists.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things to separate. One is whether there are legitimate national security concerns around AI, and the other is whether the particular framing Dario uses is helpful. You can take the first seriously without agreeing with the second.

When the CEO of an AI company warns about a foreign competitor, we should scrutinize the argument. They may sincerely believe it, but their company also benefits from policies that constrain competitors. That doesn’t make the warning wrong; it means we need specific evidence and a clear account of what policy would actually reduce the risk.

My concern with framing this primarily as a race against China is that it can make cooperation harder and encourage people to justify moving faster on safety grounds. I’d rather discuss concrete capabilities, concrete risks, and safeguards that should apply regardless of where a model is developed.

r001.rationale: The response questions the China-race framing but does not address near-term risks from open-weight AI models or judge Amodei’s warnings about them overly forceful.
